h: More of mid Cornwall to explore
p: Eden makes a cracking base for exploring this part of the county, because so much of the area's story is tied to the same china clay that left behind the pit the Biomes now sit in. To get to grips with that history, Wheal Martyn just north of St Austell is a museum set around a preserved clay works, with waterwheels, old machinery and woodland trails. It's a great companion visit, especially if the kids have asked why Eden is in a giant hole.

Garden lovers are spoilt for choice nearby. The Lost Gardens of Heligan, near Mevagissey, were rediscovered and restored after decades of neglect and are packed with jungle valleys, productive Victorian gardens and woodland walks. Mevagissey itself is a working fishing harbour with narrow lanes, pasty shops and boat trips in season.

Back at Eden, a few tips make a big difference. The site is built into a steep-sided pit, so expect slopes and plenty of walking; if anyone in your group has limited mobility, have a chat with the team about accessible routes. Arrive with a rough plan of what you want to see so you're not doubling back. In summer, look out for the Eden Sessions concerts, when big-name acts play against the backdrop of the Biomes.
Food-wise, there are cafés on site, but a picnic on the grass outside works beautifully on a fine day. Bring a reusable bottle, as you'll get thirsty in that rainforest.
And if it's chucking it down, don't panic. The Biomes are the best place in Cornwall to be on a soggy day.
